correctness.rationale: For prescribed alternating gradients, y_t=v_t/G² obeys y_t=y_(t−1)−s sign(y_(t−1)−1), s=1−β₂>0. Starting at zero it advances by s until it reaches or crosses one. At integer q=1/s it reaches one and sticks; otherwise it visits Ns and (N+1)s in alternating order from N=floor(q), with Ns on parity N. Direct substitution gives m_t=p[(-1)^(t−1)+β₁^t], p=(1−β₁)G/(1+β₁), including m_0=0. The β₁^t contribution is absolutely summable since the reciprocal denominator is bounded by 1/ε. The eventual periodic part of the normalized update has mean p(-1)^(N−1)Δ/2, so multiplication by −η gives the stated slope and bounded remainder. For exact locking or the separate initialization v_0=G², the denominator is eventually constant and the alternating part has zero mean. The exact decimal settings give q=10,100,1000. The argument is analytic; the packaged floating-point transcription guards were read, not executed. This is exact-real, constant-rate, prescribed-input analysis of the algorithm as printed, not a claim about gradients along a fixed objective, bias-corrected implementations, or exact locking in machine arithmetic.

value.rationale: An exactly zero pair-sum input is a motivated diagnostic of whether adaptive normalization preserves cancellation. The result identifies an exact parameter boundary and phase-controlled direction of steady motion, distinguishing harmless oscillation in a denominator from its effect on a balanced signed signal. It also shows why the paper's exact decimal settings mask the diagnostic and why matched initialization suppresses it. This is a useful counterexample to cancellation at constant learning rate, not a claim of realistic optimization failure or evidence against the paper's stochastic convergence theorem.
